That way, you can build serious strength from home with no gym required. Dip bars are also excellent for building lats and back with rows, levers, and body weight curls. The other issue is that gymnastic rings are not as beginner friendly and have a much steeper learning curve. And while they're excellent for developing stability, functional strength, propriception, all that good stuff, you can't add additional weight as easily or safely, making them less suitable for strength training or hypertrophy. And I wouldn't fancy doing advanced calisthenics skills with gymnastic rings like PL training or handstands for that very same reason. So yeah, I love gymnastic rings, but dip bars are my top choice. === FILE: Advanced Isometric Training： Ballistic and Quasi Isometrics [Gp2AMkdXM90].en.txt ===

i love cool lesser talked about types of training that can help you to achieve awesome results isometrics ticks all those boxes and then some and in this post i'm going to share two even lesser known forms of isometrics that might make a huge difference to your strength gains but first a quick recap so isometrics are contractions with no movement these come in two flavors overcoming isometrics and yielding isometrics the former refers to an isometric contraction against an immovable object trying to bend an iron bar for instance or push down a tree like the indian wrestler gamma the latter kind yielding isometrics refers to any attempt to hold a position against resistance such as when holding a handstand or keeping a barbell halfway above your chest with arms bent during a bench press both kinds of contraction have their benefits but it's overcoming isometrics that will help you to increase your max strength without necessarily increasing muscle size this is accomplished by increasing your ability to recruit motor units in the muscle in other words the nervous system adapts to enable you to use your muscles more totally this also occurs during one rep max here you use 100 of your available force to move a weight thus training yourself to use your muscle at maximum efficiency but the limitation here is that during a one rep maximum that maximum force within the muscle only occurs for a couple of milliseconds at the most difficult point of the movement what sets an overcoming isometric apart is that this maximum contraction is continuous allowing for a truly max effort over an extended period the results speak for themselves most old-time strongmen used some form of overcoming isometrics modern strongman dennis rodgers has done the same thing to the point of exceeding even elite athletes in his motor recruitment as i've discussed often this was also a key component of bruce lee's training to utilize overcoming isometrics to their fullest you should aim to concepts so that you start the contraction as explosively as possible and then hold it for a little while after but there's another interesting way to incorporate ballistic isometrics too because if left in reserve to prevent injury and to conserve energy so as you start to fatigue the motor units you're currently using you can send a new neural drive to recruit even more large ones in doing so you dig deeper recruit more strength and force more neural adaptations so this is a great hack for building even more strength from isometrics at the other end of the spectrum we have quasi-isometrics press-up this is much harder than it may at first sound but it does numerous things firstly it trains you to much more finely control the amount of force that you're exerting during the movement you continuously during the stretched position which is well known to elicit hypertrophy and strength gains in short if overcoming an explosive isometrics build brute force and power quasi isometrics can be used to develop finesse and precision combine both and you can begin to control your muscles in a way that even strength athletes rarely manage to get started aim for around thirty percent of your one rep max or use body weight to avoid injury then aim for a 30 second contraction and the same for eccentric obviously if you can't manage that right away 15 seconds 20 seconds that's fine this is control as possible passive means you're attempting to relax and use only the necessary strength the former is better for hypertrophy effectively being very similar to a negative rep or a weighted complex movements that put you in a compromised position this technique is not suitable for deadlifts for instance a good way to use them is at the end of a workout as a kind of finisher you can also when running Barefoot most experts and proponents agree that using a forefoot strike is preferable this allows the feet and knees to absorb the impact like a spring however this is less clear-cut when walking some people argue that the same logic applies the forefoot strike or midfoot strike means the knee is less locked out on impact and the foot is closer to the center of gravity the only problem is that there isn't much evidence to back this up not only do many barefoot cultures still walk with a heel strike but it appears we have anatomical adaptations that favor the heel strike for example when the heel touches the floor this triggers a reflex that engages the anterior tibialis the shin muscle slows and controls the foot's downward motion which is not to say that you can't use a more gentle heel touch as you lower your foot and bring your feet closer to your body with slightly shorter strides what do you think ultimately what works for one person might be different from what works from someone else I'd love to hear your ideas bye for now

=== FILE: Bruce Lee's Training & Workouts [uHc4086gn9M].en.txt ===

To many people, Bruce Lee represents the absolute peak in human physical performance and athleticism. He was renowned for his incredibly low body fat, which gave him this wicked looking physique. But what was much more impressive than the way his physique looked was what it could do. Bruce Lee was capable of some incredible feats of power. And he may well have been one of the strongest people alive pound-for-pound during his lifetime. So, let's take a look at the way Bruce Lee trained. see if we can learn something from his notes and see if perhaps we can apply some of the principles he used to our own training methods. The first thing that makes Bruce Lee unique among his contemporaries was the fact that he trained with weights at all. At the time, most martial artists believed that if they trained with weights, it would make their muscles big and bulky and slow, and this would make them less effective as fighters. Bruce Lee did the research, however, and he knew that he could use martial arts training in combination with bodybuilding and powerlifting type techniques in order to develop more explosive power through that fast twitch muscle fiber and that mind muscle connection. And that's what his training was all about. He wasn't really interested in building size. He was much more interested in building pure power. And so he used some quite unique training methods that um are slightly different from what you might be familiar with as a bodybuilder perhaps or just as a regular gym rat, but allowed him to build this kind of insane strength without packing on that much extra size. Recently only weighed about 135 lbs. So he's quite a small guy. But the stuff he could do with that, such as the one the two-finger push-up, such as apparently holding barbells out at arms length for long periods of time, weighing 40 kg. They demonstrate that he had an awful lot of power behind him. The first thing that really sets Bruce Lee apart is his philosophy and the emphasis he put on philosophy in his training. I've written recently about the importance of a training philosophy. And Bruce Lee epitomizes this idea. Bruce Lee didn't just train because he wanted to look good. Bruce Lee trained because he wanted to be a better fighter. And beyond that, he believed that martial arts were the perfect way to express yourself. He wanted to have the ability to be in full complete control of his body so that when he wanted to do something, it was right there so that he could be completely in sync with his emotions. He used to say when he wants to punch, you better believe he's going to punch you. So, he had to develop that speed and that power. And this was the driving force behind what he did. This is why he was so committed to training. It's why he truly believed in it. And that's why he was willing to put in so much work. He wasn't training for a goal. He was training for the love of training. He was like a real life Goku or something. always coming up with new ways to push the envelope. And that's the other thing about Bruce Lee. He didn't just settle for following a training program, hiring a personal trainer as you or I might. Instead, he was constantly experimenting with brand new techniques and pushing the envelope. Just as he developed Jeep Kundo, believing that he should do away with the classical mess of martial arts. He also didn't just follow conventional bodybuilding wisdom. He did the research. He looked into the studies and he tested on himself. In that way, he's very much like one of the earliest biohackers. He was constantly experimenting with new ways to not just gain incremental increases in strength, but to push the envelope and to actually exponentially unlock um entirely different kinds of power. And you're going to see some of the ways he did that in a second. So, in terms of just his general training program, Bruce Lee would do a fairly regular combination of compound movements, isolation movements, and CV. He did a lot of functional training. that means deadlifts and squats and um clean and presses because he believed that would give him more power. You see pictures of him doing one armed presses using the muscles in unison in order to make them more useful. But he did also do isolation training. There's lots of images and videos of him doing bicep curls. And I heard somewhere someone said if you think bicep curls aren't functional then you've obviously never wrestled. And clearly Bruce Lee agreed with that idea. On top of all that weightlifting, Bruce Lee would also do a lot of CV. Apparently, he would run nearly every single day when he could. And he was constantly adding progressive overload by running faster, doing tempo runs, trying to push his anorobic threshold, or even running with resistance, running with weights strapped to his back to make it more difficult. On top of this, he also did early interval training, which wasn't really a thing at the time. He did this in the same way that you might structure a boxing round. So, he'd do 2 minutes of intense training and then 1 minute rest, which would be the rest between rounds, and then he'd go again. Bruce Lee, like I said, was something of a pioneer, something of a da Vinci of the body, constantly discovering things ahead of his time, interval training being one of them. Now, many people recommend interval training, but like I said, he's also partial to a lot of CV and steady state CV. And the reason for this is that he believed it was better for his overall ability to continue to output energy for long periods of time. And he explained that if you're going to be a fighter, you really need this ability. It's no good to be able to punch and kick hard. If you're going to be out of breath after the third kick and then you have to lie down. He said something along the lines of if you don't have a good cardiovascular system, then you need to look into a more peaceful activity as your hobby. For that interval training, Bruce Lee would be using punches and kicks and jabs against a heavy bag, which makes sense as a martial artist. And he would also train each of his different strikes on different days, splitting them like a bodybuilder might split body parts. He'd do kicks on one days, punches on another day, etc. So when you combine all that, the running, the lifting, the striking, you realize Bruce Lee was just completely dedicated to his training, and it's no wonder that he had this incredibly low body fat and just looked like something out of a comic book because, you know, if you're going to train for those kinds of hours, then that's how you're going to end up looking. And like I said, Bruce Lee used some more interesting training methods as well. He didn't just do lifting. When he was doing his weight training, he thought a bit outside the box again. And this is where he came up with some really unique and interesting ideas. One of them being speed training. So on these days, Bruce Lee would try and increase the challenge of his workouts, but he wouldn't do it the way most of us do it by increasing the weight or by increasing the number of repetitions. Instead, he'd do it by increasing the speed at which he completed the workout. So the same workout, but try and complete it faster times. A little bit like something that CrossFitters are doing these days. But the reason this was interesting to Bruce Lee in particular is because when you use explosive fast movements, you're essentially engaging more fast twitch muscle fiber. You're telling the body it needs explosive force. And the body can't tell the difference between resistance and acceleration. Force is force. That's what it needs to generate to go fast. That's what it needs to generate to lift something heavy. So by lifting the same weights faster, as far as the muscles are concerned, it's the same thing as lifting them heavier. You'll engage more fast muscle fiber, but it probably won't result in quite the same muscle damage. and micro tears, meaning that he could potentially develop more strength without creating quite so much hypertrophy. Apart from anything else, this is just a great way to mix things up. And I recommend trying it, and you'll see right away that it definitely challenges you in a slightly different way to what you're perhaps used to. So, why not give that a go? Another thing Bruce Lee did that was quite different was he used a lot of isometric training. Isometric, of course, means that you're holding. It's the opposite of plyometric. Instead of explosive movement, you're holding one position. So, for instance, you might hold the bicep, you might hold the bicep curl position using dumbbells and then slowly allow them to drop as you completely use up all of your strength. Bruce Lee believed that because you're holding it in the point where there's the most resistance where it's the most difficult as opposed to having the arm straight or up here, you're engaging the most strength. However, at the same time, you're not going through the full range of motion. So, Bruce Lee knew that you need to combine this kind of training with regular training. what I just described there where you're holding the weight and letting it gradually fall. That's called yielding isometrics. That's where you're holding the weight and then letting yourself fatigue. But that's not the only type of isometric training Bruce Lee used. And it's also probably not the most interesting. The most interesting kind of isometrics that Bruce Lee would use was called overcoming isometrics. And here what he would do is he'd hold on to a really heavy weight that he literally couldn't lift. So, for instance, he'd lie under a bench press and he'd load up the bar to be 200 kg or 300, who knows what he can lift. And then he would just strain to try and push it. He did the same thing with squatting. He'd have a squat rack where the bar was on his neck, but it was locked in place. So, he just try and push up this bar that wasn't going anywhere. Likewise, he would do the same with curling by chaining a bar to the ground and then trying to curl it. Obviously, he could not. You hold that position for a few seconds, let it go, and try again. This is the definition of what happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object. Bruce Lee being that unstoppable force. I've actually talked about this kind of overcoming isometrics in the past. And again, what makes it interesting is its ability to recruit those faster twitch muscle fibers. when you're pushing against something that won't move or pulling against something that won't move. Again, your brain and your muscle fibers, they don't know the difference between something that's locked in place and something that's just really heavy. So, to begin with, you're just pulling and pushing as hard as you can, and you're recruiting all of the fast fast twitch muscle fibers. So, you're training your ability to exert maximum strength at a given time. Not only could this potentially strengthen those fast twitch fibers, but more importantly, it can strengthen the mind muscle connection. The mind muscle connection is a concept in bodybuilding that describes obviously the connection between the mind and the muscle through from the brain through down the nervous system through the neuromuscular junction and then to the muscle itself. When you tell yourself to move, you send the signal that travels there and then you recruit a certain amount of muscle when you need to. Different people have differing levels of muscle fiber recruitment and it tends to be anywhere between 30 and 50%. 50% being a highly trained athlete. So even a highly trained athlete can't call upon all of their muscle fibers at once because if they did they could cause injury to their tendons and ligaments and they could likewise completely fatigue themselves which in the wild would leave you completely vulnerable to predators. Dennis Rogers is a guy who can naturally by genetics call upon more muscle fiber. has been shown in studies and this gives him fantastic strength for his size. He's a small guy, but he may be currently one of the strongest men pound-for-pound. Look him up online. He does some incredible things. To me, there's always been something very satisfying about exercise that incorporates an element of locomotion, you know, movement. Essentially, massage jumping involves leaping up and down on the spot, keeping the torso vertical, and only somewhat flexing at the knees and ankles. You're bending the ankles and the knees just enough to absorb impact, but without the usual amortization phase. You're not dipping down into deep squat and leaping up like we usually associate with vertical jumping. Better yet, if you can avoid doing an arm pump. As functional coach JC Santana explains, being able to jump in sports is not about generating power from a deep squat. It's about being able to rebound energy from the ground. When we're playing sports, we jump off of one foot while running and we hardly flex at the knees at all. So it's not as much about being able to generate force from nothing as it is about translating power, translating energy upwards. And the same is true for sprinting. It will prevent jarring the knees and it will make this a more intense exercise. After each rep, jump up, spin round, and repeat in the opposite direction. If you use it correctly, the key is to perform lots of reps and to keep landing softly into that position. All those squats on your toes build up and you start to really feel a decent burn by the end. Do three sets of 10 or three sets of 15 and you will feel this. === FILE: Functional Training： Compound vs Isolation vs Calisthenics [wTRjodtd9to].en.txt ===

So, as you watch this, I'm either just about to go on holiday or I've just come back. So, life has been pretty hectic and busy. I thought I'd try and squeeze in a quick video here so that I could upload you with something and not leave you hanging whilst I was away. So, today I wanted to discuss the difference between isolation exercises, compound exercises, and calisthenics. And specifically, which ones are the best in terms of functional strength, aesthetics, etc. because a lot of people have some very strong opinions on these matters and you might find that there's some information you're not aware of that could help you to reassess those opinions. So the conventional view that a lot of people take is that compound exercises are more effective than isolation exercises. Compound exercises being multi- joint exercises. So that includes things like the squat, like the bench press, the deadlift, clean and snatch, anything where you're using multiple muscles at once in unison. So this requires coordination. It requires the muscles to work as a single unit. And that is how you use them in the real world. If you're pushing furniture around, if you're pulling down a something, I don't know what you pull down in the real world. That was a weird example. But if you're essentially using your strength in the real world, you don't just use one joint as in isolation exercises. Isolation exercises are your bicep curls, your tricep extensions, your latap pull downs. Here you are fixed into place. Lap pull downs less. So you're fixed into place and you're using just one or perhaps two joints. And that really isolates all the focus onto one muscle, but that is not how you use your muscles in the real world. So yes, like I say, a lot of people these days in particular prefer compound exercises because they think they're more functional. They think they are closer to how you'd move in the real world. Exemplifying this, you have your seven primal movements. This is the notion that there are seven basic movements on top of which all other movements can be built. So these are gate which is walking and running, lunging, squatting, bending, torque, pushing which includes vertical push and horizontal push, pulling which is vertical pull and horizontal pull. Notice that bicep curls are not on that list. So in other words, these are the movements that everyone should be able to do that we would have been able to do in the wild and that we would have used a lot during our evolution. And thus they are the most functional, the most useful and all of these compound movements involve piling lots of weight on top and then doing those movements. So squat is of course squatting. You can do a lunge. You can do gate with something like farmer's walk. You can do uh talk with this uh axe exercise using the cable pulley machine. You get the idea. And a lot of people will also tell you that compound movements are what you need to use if you want to get bigger. And the reason they cite for this is that using multiple muscle groups in unison triggers the release of more anabolic hormones like testosterone, like growth hormone. This has been shown in studies that you do release more of these hormones during exercises of that that nature. And in theory, it follows that you would build more muscle as a result. Thus, many people say that the most important thing you can do if you want to become a big bodybuilder type is to do squats and deadlifts, etc. And then you have all those crossfitters like Rich Froing who appear to support this theory. Thus, the isolation exercise, the traditional movements used by a lot of bodybuilders, the isolation curl, the tricep kick back, etc., these are going the way of the dodo, the leg extension, the hamstring curls. People are saying that these exercises aren't functional. They like to cause injury imbalances and that they don't build as much muscle. But the first thing I want to do is to defend the isolation movement because I think that there's a lot of merit in isolation movement. And it's actually something that everyone should be doing as a part of their routine. Whether or not you are interested in functional strength, whether or not you're interested in looking great. First of all, if you want to create micro tears and metabolic stress, which are the things you need in order to create hypertrophy, muscle growth in any specific area, then you do need isolation exercises. So, there are lots of theories as to how hypertrophy works. But generally, the concept is that the more you curl when you're lifting a heavy enough weight, you create tiny tears in the muscle fiber called micro tears. These then heal with satellite cells, come back thicker and stronger, the muscle gets bigger. At the same time, the muscle is also pumped with more fluids. It stores more fluids as you train for endurance in those exercises. When you do an isolation exercise such as a curl, you're focusing just on that muscle. And this really isolates it. It focuses all of those micro tears and all that metabolic stress on that muscle. When you do a exercise like a squat or a bench press, you're using so many different muscles at once that they're not focused. You're not focusing all the effort on just one. But more importantly, when you're doing an isolation exercise, you can go to failure and you can go beyond failure. So you can do as many bicep curls as you can physically do, then give up, then lower the weight and do a drop set. Continue to go. And what this does is it creates those micro tears. You pick up the lighter weight. You create even more micro tears. Meanwhile, you're swelling the area with blood, which is what's causing the metabolic stress. You're oluding it. You're preventing the blood from escaping. That's what gives you that sensation of pump. The greatest feeling you can get in the gym or the most satisfying feeling you can get in the gym is the pump. Let's say you drain your biceps. Blood is rushing into your muscles and that's what we call the pump. Your muscles get a really tight feeling like your skin is going to explode any minute. You know, it's really tight. It's like somebody blowing air into into your muscle. It just blows up and it feels different. It feels fantastic. and then you're essentially just really nuking that muscle. And you just can't do that with a multi- joint exercise. The reason being that if you're doing a squat and you start to suffer, if one muscle starts to become weaker than the others, then you have to stop. If you're squatting and your hamstrings aren't as strong as say your back or if your um glutes aren't as strong, then you'll have to put down the weight. You won't be able to complete the repetition. but none of them will have gone to failure. It's also not safe to keep going through drop sets and to aim for your one rep max without a spotter. So, you just can't create the same kind of isolated damage to the muscle that you need in order to trigger massive growth. You have to stop before you get to that point. And as for the body producing more anabolic hormones during these exercises, that actually doesn't have as much as a bearing as you might think. Studies show that the testosterone and the growth hormone that you produce during these big compound lifts and any exercise don't actually contribute to hypertrophy. So it is true that you produce more when you do the compound lifts, but it doesn't make any difference anyways. You know, when you watch an action film or when you have sex or when you see someone win a race, these are also things that trigger testosterone release in the body. And let's not forget that muscle endurance in itself is also functional. It's all very good and well being able to lift something really heavy once with a big compound lift. I'm not telling you not to do compound movements. Like I say, they are more functional. They are closer to what we would do, you know, in the wild during our evolution, but I'm also saying don't throw the baby out with the bath water. Isolation movements are still very important, especially if you're interested in hypertrophy and size. And if you're interested in building pure strength, then they're important as well because of course you're strengthening the the links in that chain and isolating the muscles that are the primary movers. At the same time, you can bring up areas that are perhaps lagging behind. You can focus on specific weaknesses in your form and your physique. So there's a lot of reason to kind of spot focus on specific muscle, whether you're interested in performance or aesthetics. So, the best way to combine these different types of training is by doing the compound movements at the start of the workout whilst you've got full strength and that'll also get you a little bit of a pre-burn on the muscles and then you can focus on specific areas following that and this lends itself particularly well to a pushpull leg split which is my preferred split but of course there are lots of different ways you can manage this. The other thing I want to address is that even compound movements aren't quite as functional as many people would assume. They are very functional. Um, but they're still practicing a very specific movement under very ideal circumstances. So, what you're doing when you do a deadlift is you're squatting down to the weight. You're picking up off the floor. You're standing up. And people say this teaches you to get better at picking things up. What it really teaches you to get better at, though, is picking up bars from a stationary position on a flat floor. Uh, in real world, whether you're helping someone move house or doing anything else, you're going to be picking up weights that are a different shape. You're going to be moving backwards whilst carrying them. You're going to be carrying them downstairs. And in the wild, you just plain wouldn't have ever done a deadlift. You wouldn't really have that much need to pick up anything heavy. If you did, it'll probably be a rock. You probably be standing on uneven ground. Your grip would be all over the place. So really, if you're training a very specific technique, that's not terribly functional. And if you're saying you need to get that technique perfectly right, otherwise you're going to injure yourself, then that's not terribly functional because again, in the wild, you need to be prepared for every different scenario. You need to be prepared for differences in the level of the ground, differences in the shape of what you're lifting. If you look at an animal, an animal doesn't warm up before it goes running. It doesn't need to use correct form. It just instinctively runs, it jumps, it fights, it lifts if it's a gorilla, but probably still nothing that heavy. And it does all this without thinking, without using correct technique. It's just so strong that it can handle all these different things. And in my recent video on oldtime strongmen, I talked about how they did the anyhow lift and all these different moves that had them moving away from the weight or lifting unusual shapes. And doing these things is a great way to build a kind of a much more functional strength. At the same time, calisthenics is very good for this because when you do calisthenics, a you're using your body as it's meant to be used. In the wild, like I said, you wouldn't really have picked up things, but what you would have done is climbed trees, jumped over ravines, um swam, done uh mounts as you climbed mountains, you'd have done press up type stuff. I guess all these types of movements are real movements and they again are very compound. They're very natural. They use all of your muscles in conjunction and to an even greater extent in many ways than a lot of the compound lifts. You try doing a plank or a handstand press up, you're using your entire core. you're controlling, you're aware of your whole body. This is an incredibly um functional type of training. When you climb a tree, you have to not only pull yourself up, but you're grabbing different widths of branches. You're clinging on at different levels. You're pulling using completely different combination of muscles on every single repetition. And that's what true functional strength is. It's adaptability. It's being able to adapt to your surroundings and not have to use a specific form. not being able to say, "I can't use my strength in this context." So, if you want to be as functional as possible, you need a rounded kind of strength. And that's actually why it's best to use all three types of training in your workouts to focus on those specific muscles and build up the strength to build those weaknesses you have in your body, to learn correct technique for complicated compound movements, to build mind muscle connection, and to be able to adapt to different situations, to use your body the way it was designed to be used. So those people who prefer one type of training to another, that's perfectly fine. But don't bemoone the others. Don't say that one is better than the other objectively because they all have their place. === FILE: How to Build Strength, Speed, Endurance in a SINGLE Workout! [gWvSCQwirfA].en.txt ===

How do you build strength, speed, endurance, and agility all at the same time? The answer is surprisingly simple. By challenging each of these traits in a single workout. Start with explosive movements when your nervous system is fresh. Move on to lifting heavy weights or using more challenging calisthenics. Then increase the reps and lower the weight to target your strength endurance. End on some mobility for greater body control. You can even combine some of these movements into a single mechanical drop set. You're now getting the endurance that comes from pumping out lots of reps, but also the strength and power from those heavier moves at the start. Some will point out that you can't get as strong as you would do when focusing purely on strength. Unless you're a competitive powerlter, that is simply irrelevant. You can still get extremely strong, and it's highly unlikely you'll need to worry about that ceiling for a long time. And what's the point of being very strong if you guess out after a minute of exertion? existing theories one reason for this is there's always the element of chance so let's say I've got a supplement called ultra strong supplement and I want to find out if it works or not before I start selling it so I give it to five participants and I look at their strengths before they start taking the supplement and afterwards if those five participants all got stronger noticeably then I might colds and so at the end of the study they were stronger than they were at the start or perhaps they were just hitting their stride at the gym or maybe some other factor led to them getting stronger I can't prove that that wasn't just a coincidence and that's why you need a much larger sample the larger the sample the less likely it is that it was just a coincidence so if I had a hundred participants and ninety nine of them got stronger moving ultra strong supplement then I might conclude that it's highly likely that they did get stronger because of this supplement the studies are forced to deal with the significance of data this basically tells you how likely it is statistically for the results to have been caused by what you were testing this is measured with the p-value where P equals naught point naught four would mean that there was a four percent likelihood that your results were a fluke generally it's considered that a significant result is five percent or below only then can research a claim that they found some kind of real-world relationship and reject their null hypothesis the prediction that nothing of note will happen what this tells you though is that when see a big study published in the news they're still possibly a 5 percent chance that it was just luck don't read the hyperbolic Daily Mail headlines then go straight to the source of the study gave the super strong supplement to people then we introduced a new workout routine at the same time there'll be a very bad design and that would be an example of a confounding variable now of course in observational studies where we're not actually interfering where we're not carrying the study out in a lab confounding variables are much more common because they can't control for every factor so we might look at people who eat lots of hot dogs and we might notice that they gain weight we spot that correlation however we haven't considered all the other factors for instance someone who eats hot dogs is also much more like to eat Mars bars is much more likely to exercise less these are confounding variables and unless we control for them by for instance forcing people who don't eat hot one of the issues when we use any kind of observational study first you can say that in a real-world setting eating more hot dogs correlates with worse health that is to say that someone who eats more hot dogs is likely to have poorer health what you cannot say though is that the hot dogs were what caused the bad health this doesn't only apply to observational studies either thus a good study should do everything it can to eliminate or account for confounding variables our study looking at diet for instance should control precisely what's being eaten make sure that the participants are getting similar amounts of exercise and generally avoid anything that might influence the outcome of the study normally this means creating a control group that means you're splitting the sample in half and only intervening with one of the two groups so you might give one group your experimental treatment and the other one no experimental treatment the idea of this is to create a group that you can compare the results to where the only difference is the new medicine or whatever variable you're testing so maybe different participants have different diets but this shouldn't be true in both groups thus by comparing the two groups and seeing if the difference is significant you can get an idea as to whether your intervention had any effect while researchers should know better they will often still jump to conclusions and claim that a causal link was found when really they've only shown a correlation is the study you're reading guilty of that the placebo effect one of the biggest confounding variables that researchers have to contend with in research is the perceiver effect the placebo effect is what happens when a participant feels differently because they believe they will be give someone a new drug to treat their flu and they'll be optimistic that they're going to get better that alone can then improve their immune system and the result will be a faster recovery solution then is to use a blind study meaning the control group will receive a sugar pill and the experimental group will get the real treatment only they don't know which one they're getting thus the placebo should affect both groups equally so any difference can be considered the result of the active ingredients or the lifestyle changes or whatever it is you're testing so in a double-blind experiment the researchers don't know which of the groups is the experimental group in which is the control group and neither of course do the subjects this is so that the researchers can't accidentally introduce any kind of bias through their knowledge of the experiment for instance it might be that the experimenter goes to the experimental group and says so have you noticed any benefits yet and then they go to the control group when they go so notice any benefits yet probs not and that subtle difference could influence the way that the participants view the experiment and therefore we might see the placebo effects being stronger in the experimental group than in the control group so if neither party if nobody knows who's the experimental group and who's the control group then there's no chance of that happening long attitudinal studies you also need to consider the length of the study how long was this new diet and exercise regime trial before it was concluded that it worked or didn't work sometimes a new diet can cause positive effects in the short-term like weight loss but very negative effects in the long-term like death if you were to study the starve yourself diet for two days you'd probably say it was very effective longitudinal studies then are very useful as they monitor their participants over very long periods of time sometimes their entire lifetimes of course these studies are also largely impractical however so they are fewer and further in between another problem with the longitudinal studies is that they can't take place in the lab === FILE: How to Train Loaded Carries With Kettlebells for Strength Endurance and Stability [HSGPWxWl1LI].en.txt ===

The Kettle Bell Loaded carry all you're doing here is carrying one or two kettle bells by your sides and going for a walk I like to use a finger grip which gets the forearms pumped and you should also maintain a slight shrug in the traps not exaggerated but just don't let your arms hang like dead weights by your side try and keep your torso straight and avoid rocking from side to side as you walk this movement can be done for distance or for time or you can increase the weight to progress this builds a massive strength endurance and mental toughness while also training the forearms traps core and hips they improve your gate cycle while also challenging you with a movement that you genuinely have to perform in the real world and for added benefit doing a one-sided carry called a suitcase carry or a briefcase carry will add to that anti- lateral flexion and this strengthens the ql the glutes and the obliques to provide further stability if you don't have space to take your C bells for a walk or don't want to go outside stand on the spot and raise your legs to do slow marching A's or 100 UPS try and keep your torso in the kettle bells as still as you possibly can while switching legs

Whether it's picking up compost when my wife goes shopping at the garden center, whether it's picking up my child when he's fallen out of bed repeatedly, whatever the case, you often find yourself picking stuff up off the floor. This is why deadlifts and other hip hinge movements are so important to incorporate into your training. I'm often tempted to go 99% body weight training, cuz I love body weightight training. But one of the things that would be missing from that style of training if that's all I did would be picking things up off the floor. There are ways I can train a hip hinge. There are ways I can train my glutes. But picking stuff up off the floor is different because you need to brace your core in a way that you just don't do when you're doing, for example, reverse hypers. And that's why I think that a complete functional training program will always need to involve some kind of weightlifting. But I also think that the deadlift isn't quite enough in this capacity. Because whilst the deadlift is an excellent movement, it doesn't that closely mimic the many different ways you can end up picking something up off the floor. When you drop something on the ground, you don't perform a perfect deadlift with a straight back and hip hinge to pick it up off the ground. Again, often you'll need to pick up something that's much lower. You'll need to round the back a little bit. Often you'll have one foot in front of the other. Often you'll be on an uneven surface. Often you'll have your feet staggered a little bit. And that's why even if you're someone who has an incredible deadlift, you can still end up hurting your back trying to pick up something really small like a sock. And as we're going to see, mobility and endurance also play a really big role in this. So, if you're training in order to pick stuff off the ground in a useful, practical manner outside of the gym, or whether you're hoping it's going to transfer optimally to things like jumping height and that kind of stuff, then you're going to want to stick around and learn some of the other methods you can use to train this important ability. And what's more is that some of these methods don't require huge amounts of weight in the same way that practicing a deadlift does, which to me is always a big bonus cuz it means you can train it from home. So, yeah, one of the first and biggest misconceptions when it comes to picking stuff up off the floor is that in order to prevent yourself getting injured, in order to get really good at this, what you're going to need is max strength and max strength alone. Now, obviously, max strength is going to massively help you with lifting things up off the ground. It's going to allow you to lift more things up, and it's going to give you a huge kind of buffer, this massive capacity. You'll be so strong in all your supporting muscles, you'll be so good at bracing, etc., that a small miscalculation is less likely to injure you. It will fortify you against injury, but it's only one part of the equation because what's also important is endurance. In the real world, outside the gym, you very, very rarely have to pick up your one rep maximum. In fact, I'd wager that you likely never will have to. What you will have to do, though, is pick up something frequently, repeatedly, a lot, after a long day of doing other stuff without a proper warm-up sometimes. And this is when things can go wrong. This is when one of those small stabilizing muscles can give out leading to massive back spasms and other issues. So, for example, one time I put my back out was after carrying my daughter on my back all day, picking her up, putting her back down, picking her up, putting her back down, and then eventually it just went out. I think I was goofing around, sprinting with her on my back, and it just went out. It's because it was tired. It's not because she's too heavy for me. I can very easily pick up that amount of weight. So, just getting stronger and stronger clearly isn't the issue. What you want to do then is train with some endurance so that you get used to using these muscles for longer duration so they get better at recovery so they have more blood supply so that you can ingrain positive movement patterns so that even when you're tired you're still moving correctly. So for example that's where something like the kettle bell swing comes in so handy. This is an exercise designed to be performed for those higher rep ranges. Meaning you're training yourself to not gas out and to maintain proper structure and form even as you get more tired. Another way you should be training strength endurance in this way is by picking stuff up but then walking with it as well because again when we actually pick up things outside of the gym, we don't put them straight back down. That's almost always going to be completely pointless. So what we do instead is we pick up something and we walk with it some distance. Whether we're moving furniture, whether we're gardening, playing with the kids, whatever it is, we're going to move that stuff a distance. So again, this is what you want to be training. We all know the many, many benefits of loaded carries of the various different ways you can load yourself on one side like a briefcase carry or both sides or even overhead. So combining this with lifting, you can even walk a distance, put it down, pick it up, walk a distance, put it down, pick it up. These are great ways to train real functional strength. What you're going to find here is, of course, you're going to be working with a lighter weight, but for longer, rather than a much heavier weight, but for a shorter amount of time. And again, this is how you use weights. We use lighter weights for longer far more frequently than we use very, very heavy weights for not as long. And the other benefit of the Cbell swing is, of course, that it's ballistic. It's an explosive movement. You're swinging the weight up using that hip hinge, but in a manner that almost mimics jumping. And this is why it can be so effective for improving sprinting and jumping. Deadlifting a heavy weight is exceptionally good for increasing jump height and running speed. This is something that Liam Ellis, the parkour athlete who contributes to this channel, talks about and it's something that's been shown in countless studies. So, as you can see, when picking stuff up off the floor, we don't just want to train max strength. We want to train endurance and explosiveness as well. But that's still not the complete package. We're also going to need chaos training or ecological training. === FILE: Plyometric Training Explained In Depth [E8a-jQjmzXM].en.txt ===

being strong and being explosive are not the same thing a strong individual is someone who can move something extremely heavy from point a to point b an explosive individual is somebody capable of running fast changing direction quickly and jumping high into the air they can also deliver snappy punches and throw things long distances they exert strength but they do so very quickly how do you become more explosive then the first place many people will turn to is plyometric training however there's a lot of confusion surrounding what plyometric training actually is and what it isn't there's even more confusion surrounding how to use it effectively and when to turn to other similar tools so let's jump in jump like in plyometric box jumps plyometric exercises utilize rapid bursts of power with a minimal ground contact time in order to utilize the stretch shortening cycle an example is a counter movement jump here the athlete lowers themselves rapidly eccentric phase pauses extremely briefly amortization phase then springs up into the air to land on a box or other raised platform concentric phase the term plyometric is a little nebulous and open to interpretation however the stretch shortening cycle means that you're lengthening and then contracting the working muscles in a very short time frame this is something we do intuitively all the time such as when you wind up a punch this is often described as being a way to tap into the stored energy that comes from stretching the muscle like an elastic band this is incorrect however in fact the power of the stretch shortening cycle appears to come from the time the muscle spends in the active state this allows for more cross bridges to form inside the muscles thereby giving the more traction as it were to then exert force the lengthening phase therefore acts more like a run-up but spend too long in the stretch position and you'll lose some of that potential because you're no longer active that's why it's harder and not easier to jump out of a squat unless you just dropped into it very briefly the former is an isometric concentric movement the latter is a plyometric concentric movement this also means that the ground contact time is actually not as important as the time the muscles spend in the active state thus a counter movement jump from the ground is still plyometric that said there is also benefits to minimizing ground contact time in other scenarios if you want to become truly explosive enter the verkoshansky depth jump and shock training the best example is the verkoshansky depth jump this involves jumping off a raised platform around 42 inches for maximum benefit and then launching back off the ground after less than 0.2 seconds this collision engages the myotatic stretch response the sudden lengthening of the muscles causes them to then rapidly contract in response and this in turn allows the athlete to draw upon huge reserves of explosive strength this same collision is also seen in sprinting over time practicing this will increase the athlete's eccentric strength as well as training the central nervous system to anticipate the myotactic reflex and thus increase firing rate in short athletes get a lot more explosive and in one study volleyball players were shown to gain a 14 increase in jump height using a depth jump program by the way if you want to see all the would need to jump on each repetition while keeping the time on the ground to 0.2 seconds or below all while properly absorbing the impact to avoid injury this could translate to even more explosive punching and throwing and have useful benefit for max bench press that said there are also some rebound elements involved in most explosive movements this is where athletic properties such as ankle stiffness become important tendon hysteresis describes how pliable a tendon is where lower hysteresis equals less pliability when running an athlete's calf actually plays a somewhat minimal role during plantar flexion as a lot of energy is returned by the stiffness of the tendon thus it can make more sense to think of the muscles in terms of muscle tendon units fascia the thin film wrap that covers the muscles organs and more which i mentioned in almost every single video also has elastic properties and is able to return energy to the ground think of it like being coated in a thin layer of flubber one of the most crucial things to understand when utilizing plyometrics is inter-serial rest periods rest times between sets if you are programming plyometrics or shock training then you should also include sufficient rest time this is not quite as straightforward as some vocal individuals on the web would have you believe however the argument goes that in order to trigger useful adaptations with plyometrics you need a long recovery period this then allows the individual to exert 100 of their max effort during each rep when performing plyometrics it has been suggested that this should be in the region of two to five minutes of intercept rest however other studies call into question just how strictly we should adhere to this one study for example found meaningful improvements in athletes using 30 60 and 120 second rest periods there was no significant difference between those groups that said going longer during inter-serial rest periods still makes a lot of sense and is generally standard practice the argument for longer rest periods is that if you don't rest sufficiently then you won't be able to call upon your max effort when you perform subsequent reps of jumps that's the key here max effort jumping as high as possible is akin to performing your one rep max you're giving a hundred percent and this is what you need to do if you want to increase jump height and rapid force production to jump higher you need to create the demand for jumping higher by regularly trying to jump as high as possible thus we should also use a similar approach to rest times and number of repetitions as though we were training with max weights number of repetitions should be somewhere in the region of four to five maximum if the aim is to increase jump height for example and rest time should be long enough to ensure max effort the next go round the number of repetitions is also limited by the amount of time we can spend performing a set of plyometrics after all this is a form of train that uses the phosphogen lactic acid or atp creatine system for rapid energy release that means we can't maintain good effort for much longer than 10 seconds how many reps can you cram into that time to answer that we must also consider the intra serial rest time in other words how long should you pause between each repetition we already know the answer if we're talking about depth jumps and shock training 0.2 seconds otherwise the intra-serial rest will be determined by the nature of the exercise itself there is an unavoidable rest period in counter-movement jumps for example of course fatigue also increases the likelihood of injury this is particularly important in any exercise that involves leaping off of heights and absorbing large amounts of shock should the athletes slip or allow their knee to collapse inwards it's game over this is true in general when using plyometrics and especially things like box jumps make sure that there are no valgus knees and that you are properly absorbing the shock as you land but it's also important to realize that training plyometrics at higher rep ranges and with less recovery is not pointless as some would have you believe for one this trains the ability to call upon explosive force even in a fatigued state this of course is how we are often required to be explosive in sports and in life we can also combine plyometrics with strength training the problem with strength training for increasing running speed is that the ground contact time for a sprinter is around 90 milliseconds this is not enough === FILE: Specificity in Functional Training： Better Exercise Selection for Sports, Athletics, MMA, & More [CFMN8lPejxo].en.txt ===

the principle of specificity refers to the widely accepted notion that the most useful exercises are those that closely match the activities they seek to train this refers not only to biomechanics but also energy systems and all other aspects in other words the best way to get better at chopping wood is to practice chopping wood the next best way is to use the cable wood chop bicep curls not so useful a good sports coach must therefore select their exercises through the lens of specificity alternatively a movement may be chosen that develops the underlying physical attributes that contribute to that movement such as isolation work for a crucial muscle group finally general physical preparedness may be used insofar as it helps to balance out the physique prevent injury and contribute to an overall more healthy individual conditioning time is limited so every exercise needs a good reason to exist in the program coaches will likewise typically increase the specificity as they get closer to the competition date thus functional coaches like jc santana of the institute of human performance advocate for the use of exercises like the truck push in favor of squats for improving running speeds and jumping heights this is predicated on his observation that the truck push involves more similar joint angles and train such attributes as ankle stiffness at approximately 90 degrees in short this provides what we refer to as superior transference the skill trained more closely matches the intended outcome squats aren't bad they're just sub-optimal by comparison when the goal is specifically to improve running speed but not everyone agrees that this is the best strategy there's an alternative viewpoint that training with exercises too similar to the skills targeted could actually be detrimental to an athlete's performance the reason for this being that they may lead to interference interference means that a new skill or movement pattern can actually complicate an existing one two similar movement patterns could conceivably confuse the athlete causing them to harm their own performance critics of functional training such as mark riptoe thus argue that the better strategy is to train an athlete's general strength and then to pile skills training on top of that ripton his followers believe that the compound barbell lifts are all you need alongside skills training crypto believes that strength is a universal property that you're either strong or you're not and that thus being strong in the squat means you're strong full stop he also believes that traits like higher fast twitch fibers are so largely genetic that all we can do is to train for strength and hope that that helps our skill this i believe is misguided neural maps aside the truth is that the traditional barbell lefts alone failed to train the different planes of motion and myriad muscles involved in useful movements generally as agreed for example that twitch fiber density is roughly 50 genetically predetermined that leaves 50 wiggle room fascinatingly our level of plasticity itself also actually seems to be genetic to an extent and other things like blood supply tendon hysteresis all of these can be trained to an extent and many of these aspects also contribute to explosiveness more to the point if strength gains really were global bodybuilders wouldn't need to train with isolation in fact you would only need one exercise you could just perform the squat the simple fact is that you can't get stronger obliques without some form of twisting or at least antilateral flexion without using the muscle group in question you can't expect to cause metabolic stress muscle damage etc and the notion that squats and other compound moves trigger such a huge release of testosterone that it results in more muscle building throughout the body is actually also mistaken the surgeon testosterone we see during training is temporary like the surge experience when watching an action movie and there are studies showing that this does not contribute to hypertrophy if you want to see these studies for any of this then click on the link in the description down exercises training endurance and work capacity would undoubtedly be more useful for the vast majority of competitive sports if you had to choose this is not to say squatting is useless far from it squats improve mobility they build core strength they develop amazing strength in the posterior chain and they increase bone density but they alone are not sufficient to provide the necessary one-legged strength the stability tendon hysteresis etc that is necessary for optimal athletic training something like skipping car pushes hill sprints or similar on the other hand do provide those necessary attributes and traits and yet interference is a known phenomenon amongst neuroscientists we can't just write this off it's referred to in the context of memory retrieval in particular but it's also believed to affect motor learning think about learning two new languages at once or even switching from the controls of one computer game to another how about when the y-axis is inverted one study possibly demonstrates the interference principle in action here professional swimmers were found to have a lower jumping height than members of the general population even those considered to be unathletic so does training with exercises that more closely mimic the desired movement actually confused the neural maps is there some kind of strange grey area where a movement is too specific but without being specific enough there is good evidence showing that the sled's pull does improve running speed ground contact time and stride length this same study also showed that the benefits were greatest when pulling approximately 75 of body weight as this increased the athlete slowed down and the technique changed resulting in less performance again a subtle difference in training drastically alters the outcomes where do we draw the line one consideration is that different sports may require differing levels of specificity the sprinter will use far more consistent technique during every competition they are running in a straight line on a flat consistent surface the same is true for a rower placed firmly on the spot and required to perform the same rowing piston movement with perfect precision power and endurance compare this with a football player who needs to constantly change speed change direction adjust to changes in the ground and often all while dribbling a ball or making split-second changes in tactics the football player isn't learning one set of biomechanics but rather infinite unpredictable permutations but perhaps the best technique is no technique that's because no two movements are ever truly the same consider that when a row arose every single stroke will be affected by their levels of fatigue in each individual motor unit altering the recruitment and coordination of muscles they'll also be affected by the effort of their teammates how still the water is the wind the weight of the boat the momentum from previous stroke this is why no rowing machine could ever truly match the experience of actually rowing we tend to think of force production as being all about output but this is far from the truth input is equally important to refine the movement producing the force this is our motor perceptual landscape and it is critical in all athletic performance and graceful movement so i ask you how can a somewhat similar exercise interfere with a movement pattern that doesn't exist a movement pattern that is in truth already an infinite number of somewhat similar but slightly different movement patterns in fact how do we even we're starting off in a slightly different position every time we get up this is what nikolai bernstein refers to as the degrees of freedom problem he concluded that we store general movement patterns this helps us to narrow down the perfect movement for the situation your body knows which version of the movement pattern to utilize because it is guided by your objectives and the shape of the === FILE: The DANGER of Fitness Dogmatism - It's a Trap! [TguBhD3ZQQo].en.txt ===

In many ways, I think that dogmatism is destroying fitness information online. Now, that might seem like a bit of a sweeping dramatic statement. Maybe I am just feeling a bit extra today, but I think I can back it up because essentially what I say so often boils down to the same thing. It's not that I'm telling you what I think you should do. In fact, I'm quite against that. What I'm telling you is to consider other options. What I'm trying to tell you is that we don't know enough to make sweeping statements about what is the optimal training for every single person. And yet so many people seem to believe otherwise. They have their thing and then they are adamant that that method or their favorite exercise is best and everything else is just a waste of time. You hear it over and over again ironically about completely different stuff. And what's so frustrating is they often come to this conclusion because they've just watched a few videos telling them that. Then they go around the internet commenting on other videos and telling them that they're wrong. Science proves that you only need this one exercise or that only this method works. No way that information could have been misrepresented to them. No way that that could be not the whole story. I mean, I've only done this my whole life. But to be clear, I'm not trying to say that I know better than anyone. I'm not bragging. All I've learned and what I want to convey to you is how much I don't know. How much all of us don't know. Consider a response to my recent video on training legs. I said in that video that most people don't need to train heavy on their legs. They don't need to lift heavy weights or to make it 2/3 of their training. Not that it isn't good, but that they don't need to. For health purposes, they can do mobility work. And for performance, they can get a lot from explosive leg training, body weightight training, running, anything like that. Now, I expected some push back to this and actually it wasn't as bad as I thought it might be. But the people that did have a problem with my philosophy represent exactly what I'm talking about here because there were those comments telling me that no, squats are the single best exercise. Everyone should perform them. Doing anything else is just avoiding hard work, making excuses, coping. Strength, after all, is the foundation of all human performance. And your legs are the most powerful part of your body. So, what possible reason would you have not to train them? Now, this sounds like a moral stance, and I've been accused of not being a serious fitness YouTuber when I tell people to consider doing alternatives like kettlebell swings or goblet squats depending on your goals. Someone said I was just going to keep beginners stuck as beginners. But that's even when I explain the benefits of kettle bell swings are different. I'm not trying to claim that they are better for max strength, but they are more ballistic and they do provide a good combination of cardiovascular training and strength training. One that will help to give you a more ripped physique as a result and give you endurance to actually perform in sports or labor. It's that happy middle ground that covers both things. Kettle bell swings aren't better than squats. They're just different and therefore better for some people depending on their goals and maybe more fun for you, maybe not. People just can't fathom that maybe absolute strength isn't the only goal. Even when I lead with that, these people can't touch their toes. They get out of breath climbing the stairs, but they'll tell you off for neglecting squats and again act like this is a matter of morality, which is completely illogical. By the way, guys, just like to take a moment to tell you about today's sponsor, NordVPN. NordVPN is a virtual private network which is a tool you can use to protect your internet browsing. It works by letting you connect to a server located elsewhere which hides your IP address and browsing activity from any near dwells that might be listening in. It's just one part of what should be a more comprehensive approach to internet security, but it's an important tool and it has many uses. One example of how this might protect your data is against a man-in-the-middle attack. This is an attack that can occur when you connect to a public Wi-Fi like in a coffee shop. And if someone who wants your data happens to be connected to the same network, they can potentially listen in on your traffic, unless you're using a VPN, in which case all they'll see is that you connected to that server. In the same comment section, someone told me that squats were categorically the best exercise for jump height and that whatever else I was saying was nonsense because science proved it. Don't you know? I told them actually when you're playing sports, you usually jump from running. That means you don't have time to stop and to go through that amortization phase to squat down on both feet and then leap up in the air. You jump off of one leg. And this isn't actually about power or strength at all. It's about translating energy upwards using the elastic recoil of the tendons. If you look, there's not much flexion at all going on. I learned this from worldrenowned functional trainer Jason Santana, and it was a real light bulb moment for me, which is maybe why I bring it up at every possible opportunity. But then this guy counters that no, despite everything I just said, despite the appearance of the movement being different, the range of motion being different, studies categorically show that squatting is best for jump height. And that would make sense because strength is so fundamental to performance. So, everybody needs to do squats. Of course, that entirely missed my point because how do you think they measure jump height in those studies as a standing countermovement jump? In other words, they stand on the spot, squat down, and leap straight up. Exactly not how you jump when you're playing sports. And when you look at studies that actually do look at the way you jump playing sports, they find that other techniques, things like plyometric training are as effective and even in some cases more so. It's missing so much nuance to forget that there's more than one type of jumping, more than one kind of jump. And we know that training ankle stiffness has similar benefits, too. All with significantly less recovery and fatigue than squatting, which is something you need to take into account when programming. And at the risk of repeating myself, I also take issue in principle with people using the argument of running faster and jumping higher as their reason for doing this exercise or that exercise if they don't ever actually run or jump inside the gym or otherwise. I've actually just had another comment on that leg training video saying that the whole video was just me making excuses to be okay with avoiding hard training. How weak, they said. Now, I hope I don't come across as a bit petty responding to comments like this, but it is a great example of this myopic mindset again, this dogmatism, because I clearly am not afraid of hard training. I have a fitness YouTube channel. In that very video, I'm doing sequences of pistol squats and squats, which not only hard to do, they were also very hard to learn and took a lot of time and dedication. But this simply reveals that that person can't appreciate hard training unless it's the hard training that they think is worthwhile. I would even argue that a lot of people view a lot of weightlifting as a way to avoid doing cardio because cardio is hard work for a lot of people. Again, this isn't to say that squats aren't extremely powerful, just that they're not the best for everything or every scenario, because nothing is the best for everything and every scenario. Nah, squats are the best for ever. And there's going to be flutes playing and trombones and flowers and garlands of fresh herbs and we will dance. But this is the kind of myopia you see all the time in discussions around fitness and performance. And this is the kind of mislication of science. Scientific studies lack nuance by design. They need to remove confounding variables that might skew results. They're attempting to test a precise relationship or to compare two different scenarios. Can you build more muscle by doing higher reps or lower reps? All other things being equal. They might take some untrained individuals, get them to perform leg curls, and see who grows bigger hamstrings, for example. That is good science. Bad science is then taking those results and applying them to every possible scenario, which is where the researchers themselves start slapping their heads. Assuming that the study is entirely watertight, which it almost certainly isn't. This is why we repeat the same studies over and over. What if high reps work better for trained athletes and low reps work better for untrained or vice versa? What if high reps work better for certain muscle groups? What if high reps work best when combined with low reps? What if high reps work better for someone who has previously done heavy weights and therefore comes closer to maxing out their fast twitch fiber? These are called moderating variables and ultimately it means that it's not accurate to say that science proves this or that about exercise because when you reintroduce the moderating variables, you can see how it can be changed to happen differently. We will never be able to test every single possible scenario because the human body is far too complex for that. We might see a study suggesting that three sets of bicep curls is better than doing two sets. But is that still true if you're also doing chin-ups in the same workout? You know, doing three sets of bicep curls, isn't that different from doing bicep curls, hammer curls, and chin-ups for the biceps? Does doing a massive drop set change the outcome as well? It's such an obvious thing to miss the fact that some exercises overlap, and yet people do. simply taking the studies exactly at face value. And the truth is we still don't know much conclusively about hypertrophy at all, the mechanisms of it. We know some of the factors and the processes involved, but there are many nuances and mechanisms we don't fully understand. And there are huge aspects of training performance that are completely ignored by the majority of content on YouTube. Like the affforementioned elastic recoil of the tendons, like the fact that connective tissue makes up 30% of muscle mass, like angioenesis, the fact that we can permanently increase blood flow to the muscles, thereby improve recovery, hypertrophy, injury prevention, strength, endurance, and more. Things like sympathetic tone. All of these are really interesting topics that just don't get explored and that mitigate so much of what we know. When someone says a rep range is best or an exercise is best, they're typically ignoring all these things and looking instead at a single metric. How big did muscle get? Just like they typically ignore entire planes of motion, body parts, and energy systems. The very same people preaching that everyone needs to do squats or whatever exercise it is are almost always ignoring rotational strength, the ability to produce power in the transverse plane. I've talked about this on this channel a lot. It's incredibly important for everything from throwing to grappling to pulling and pushing to punching to lifting at awkward angles. So why would someone preach that you have to train the big three lifts while completely ignoring things like cardio, mobility, other forms of hypertrophy or entire planes of motion? Where does this cognitive dissonance come from? Again, the answer is dogmatism, group think, and human nature. You know, partly it's just people being extremely competitive, wanting to be the best, especially guys a lot of the time. So many people want to be the very best at what they do. They want to be the strongest, the toughest, the best fighter, the most alpha. === FILE: The Many Benefits of 5-10 Minute Cardio (Micro Cardio) [brRj6KjonNU].en.txt ===

Short bouts of cardio for just 5 minutes could be the catalyst you need to start getting the results you want from your training. Here's why. Many people only think of cardio in terms of losing fat, perhaps improving their running times, and maybe even how it can harm their muscle. But that's a mistake because there are so many benefits to cardio. Cardio is essential for your health and fitness and improves your heart health, your metabolism, your circulation, your aerobic system, your mental health, and much more. And by doing just 5 minutes of cardio, you can actually increase your energy levels and improve your focus. You increase blood flow to your brain. You produce more awakening excitatory neurotransmitters, and you warm up your body temperature. All this can stop you feeling lethargic, and that gives you the energy you need to then attack another workout or just engage in whatever other task it is you want to perform. Because it's so short, there's a relatively low psychological barrier, and you're not going to leave yourself feeling spent and tired after the fact. And while these short bouts of cardio won't use lots of calories in themselves, they can support other weight loss strategies by providing small bursts of activity throughout the day. And at a time when many of us are largely sedentary for large portions of the day, this can be extremely valuable. Microc cardio can also be extremely beneficial from a performance perspective. If you do this a couple of times a day, it's not just about performing the cardio. It's about starting and finishing the cardio, ramping your heart rate up, and then bringing it back down to normal. This can improve your heart rate kinetics and that will make you more responsive to a wider variety of tasks with a minimal preparation. In short, making you more ready for whatever it is you want to do at any point during the day and helping you to recover from your training more effectively. For all these reasons, despite not seeming like much, microcardio can actually be highly effective. Ow! Bulls!

=== FILE: These Kettlebell Rows Train Back Health, Rotation, AND Stability! #kettlebells #shorts [hPYyyhlgY54].en.txt ===

the kettle bell bent over row has a host of variations each with different functional advantages you can perform this in a free standing bent over fashion or you can place one hand on your knee for support the former makes this an anti-rotational movement as you have to resist the weight pulling your body down towards one side whenever you push your pull with one hand you need to brace the core in the transverse plane so this is a very effective benefit plus holding this unsupported position makes it a kind of good morning giving the back boots and hamstrings a nice isometric challenge if you want to emphasize the rotational aspect then you can add extra rotation as you pull the weight up if you want to enhance the stability challenge try using ballistic alternating rows throw the kettle bell up a bit as you lift it and then catch it on the other side in front of you this way you must brace an anticipation of the force as you swap arms this works the multifidus muscles and prepares you for unexpected forces on the core which are often what cause back pain
