So, I hope you don't mind the kind of slap dash approach, but also I think it's a good way of demonstrating what I'm talking about. And I think on this occasion, hopefully the information speaks for itself. Here's what you need to know. So, as most of you are aware already, we have slow twitch muscle fiber that are weaker but have better endurance and fast twitch muscle fibers that are stronger and bigger but have less endurance. These muscle fibers are grouped together as motor units. These are the smallest usable units of muscle, each controlled by an individual nerve and each containing entirely just one type of fiber. So when you send a signal to the muscle to contract, it innovates that particular group of muscle fibers via a specific motor neuron. Now, most weight training focuses on the larger motor units that contain the fast twitch muscle fiber. These are the most involved in strength after all, and they're larger, meaning they theoretically contribute more to size. So that makes sense on paper, and this is why so many people believe that you need heavy weights to build muscle. Due to a law called Henman's size principle, we know that the body only uses the smallest and weakest muscle fiber that it needs to in order to complete a given task. It's just more efficient and it gives you more control. It then adds larger motor units as the task requires more strength and power. So, an example, if you want to lift a spoon to your mouth or to gently pet a cat, you'll only use a few smaller motor units that contain slow twitch muscle fiber. Otherwise, if you use the big ones, you'd launch the spoon into the ceiling or crush the cat, which is not what you want. When you lift a heavy weight though, you still use those same slow twitch muscle fibers, but then you add more fast twitch ones on top of that to increase the total power output. That's the part I want you to focus on here, and that's the part that no one talks about. The body never only uses the large motor units. While it can use only slow twitch muscle fibers to execute small, gentle movements, it can never only use fast twitch muscle fibers. And the easy way to understand this is that when you contract your muscle, you can only send a weak signal or a strong signal. And any signal that's strong enough to engage the bigger motor units must also engage the smaller ones. Now, as I've explained before, when we train a failure with low weight, we eventually fatigue and exhaust the slow twitch muscle fiber. At that point, we need to make more effort. So, we send a stronger signal, and this recruits the fast twitch muscle fiber to take over. This is how we can engage the fast twitch muscle fibers even with lightweight because they are all that's left. So, it is still possible to build muscle size and strength with light weight as long as you're going to failure. But, we know this. This is established and I've discussed it a whole lot on the channel already. The really interesting part and the thing that people are missing is that this style of training using light weight to failure actually does something else. Something that heavy weight training can't do. And that is it trains the slow twitch muscle fibers to failure as well as the fast twitch fibers. So, when you lift a very heavy weight, you engage the slow and fast twitch fibers, as we've discussed, but the fast twitch fibers are doing all the work. And when those fast twitch muscle fibers give up, the slow twitch fibers that remain aren't going to be enough to keep on working. So, you instantly fail and stop the movement. Let's use a real world example. When you finish a super heavy bench press, you do so because the fast twitch fiber has fatigued and given up. Even though the slow twitch fiber is relatively untouched. Put simply, you're too tired to complete another 100 kg rep, but you probably could still do a bunch of push-ups. In a sense, then you have some power left in the tank. You haven't completely trained every muscle fiber in the muscle to failure. Compare this to finishing 239 push-ups and collapsing in a heap. You now can't do a single additional push-up. In that regard, you fatigued a greater proportion of all the muscle. You wore out all of the slow twitch fibers and then all of the fast twitch ones. That's what I mean when I say this trains every muscle fiber in the muscle. Now, of course, it doesn't really. You still have the extremely slow and small motor units, you know, that you use for things like picking up a spoon. Otherwise, you wouldn't be able to move at all, which the body doesn't want. But in a practical sense, you have trained every muscle fiber that you could need to in that muscle. And coincidentally, this is why this kind of training is so efficient, why you can get away with doing just a couple of sets per body part. Oh, and before someone tells me that the studies show that high reps aren't as effective, no, they don't. Firstly, there are lots of studies showing that high rep lightweight can achieve similar results. It's just that the results do vary across studies. Moreover, though, the way these studies are conducted usually just isn't the same. Of course, if I rep out 20 light reps of something, just going through the motions, I'm not going to get the same results. You need to feel that constant tension and you need to push yourself to failure. Being sure to maintain constant tension on the muscles, using a rapid cadence, and often using drop sets. But before anyone gets mad with me, I'm not claiming this is a replacement for very heavy weight training. I'm not saying this is the one true way. Heavy lifting still offers unique benefits of its own. And in an ideal world, you'd still do both. And there's other stuff you need, too, like proper cardio and doing full range of motion mobility work, too. But with that said, depending on your goals, this might be a great option. And I think anyone can benefit from integrating this approach. But hang on a moment. Does hitting every muscle fiber like this really matter? Yeah. Firstly, because slow twitch muscle fiber still contributes to powerful movement as we've seen. It's like having a tugofwar with adults and kids. The adults being the fast twitch fibers and the kids being the slow twitch. In that tugof-war, if you have stronger kids, that will still make your team stronger overall, even if their contribution is lesser. So, in this sense, training the slow twitch muscle fiber still makes you stronger. And especially now that we know that slow twitch fiber is involved in everything from sprinting to lifting heavy weights. Not only that, but although the slow twitch muscle fibers are smaller, there's also more of them. So you actually have a roughly equivalent surface area. If you aren't training them sufficiently, then you're missing out on all that hypertrophy. You're just making the big fibers bigger, but there's only a few of them instead of making all of those smaller ones bigger as well. If you want to be functionally strong, whether in wrestling or doing manual labor or playing sports, you can't guess out after a few minutes. === FILE: Train LESS for MORE Muscle and Performance Gains - Why it Can Work [ifySaIqI5Rs].txt ===

 I think a lot of people assume that I'm literally training all the time with insane intensity. I make videos with titles like SPAM Daily Reps and Why You Should Train Every Day, I'm constantly lifting weights, running, doing all these different things. But the truth is, I actually don't train a crazy amount. What I do is I train frequently, but I don't train insanely intensely during those workouts, and my workouts themselves, I keep nice and short. In fact, if you add it all up, I actually don't train for that many hours per week, maybe three to four hours total, divided into 20, 30 and 40 minute sessions, and I think that's really important to understand if you are trying to do lots of things and you have a life outside of the gym. So how does this actually work? How can you train less and actually get more results, and how can you implement this into your lifestyle and routine in order to see the results that you want? So first we need to define what I mean by training less, because like I say, I'm not actually saying that you should train just two or three times a week. What I'm actually saying is that many people could benefit from making their workouts drastically shorter, and there's a few ways that you can do this. One is to break your workouts into smaller modules, so instead of doing one one hour workout, you instead do two 30 minute workouts. You might alternatively have a couple of bigger workouts and then smaller modules that you do throughout the week, and this is what I do personally. You can do it by using fewer exercises per workout. I think bodybuilding culture has made many of us think that we need 10 different exercises to target the biceps, 10 different exercises to target the shoulders, and this is what I used to believe as well. But if you're just interested in a certain amount of strength and performance and size, often you can do with just one per body part. Another option is to reduce the number of sets you do per exercise. This is an idea that's becoming increasingly popular, and again it depends on your goals. If it's strength endurance, then maybe you want more sets. But if your main goal is size and strength, then two is often enough, and in fact in some cases it can be superior. And finally you need to recognise when you've provided yourself with the necessary stimulus. You need to learn to recognise that stimulus and then get out of the gym and call it a day. And again of course all of this is going to depend on your goals. Some of these things are going to apply to you, some won't. So you have to decide what works best for you. But in many cases you're going to find that there's a lot of fat that can be cut from your routine without losing much value at all. And this has certainly been true for me. I've drastically reduced the number of exercises I do per workout, drastically reduced the number of sets I do per workout, and I've just seen better results thanks to that. This is one of the main ideas behind Super Functional Training 3, Super Mover, which actually just uses four to five exercises per workout in many cases. And some of those are only done for two sets. And again a lot of it comes down to so much of YouTube content being geared towards high-level bodybuilders, high-level powerlifters, maybe people using performance enhancing drugs, or at least people who want to be in those brackets. There's a law of diminishing returns. You can do one really good set for your pecs and you can see growth. And if you're not in a hurry and if you don't need to look like Arnold Schwarzenegger, that's going to be enough for most people. It's only when you want to be competing at the highest level that it then makes sense to do bench press, pec flies, incline press, decline press. All in the same workout. So it comes down to remembering precisely what your goals are and being laser focused on those. One of the things I struggle with when trying to do this is that I want to train everything. Single leg strength, rotation, frontal plane movement, grip strength. I think it's important not to leave out whole planes of motion just because they're not as glamorous. But you can still do all this and include fewer exercises than you would do if you hit every single one of the mirror muscles from five different angles. As mentioned, this is because so few people actively train or stretch the QL. They're so interested in moving up and down, forwards and backwards. Now, the problem with a lot of the advice you're going to hear with a lot of the corrective exercises people give is that they're boring and fiddly and they only offer a small stimulus. === FILE: Training Philosophy： Training vs Adaptation [9VZznslww98].en.txt ===

among the primal fitness crowd there is the notion that there's a natural optimal way to move live and train we've distanced ourselves from the environment that shaped our evolution and as such this is what has introduced so many of our modern maladies while i agree with this to some extent i do feel that it simplifies matters somewhat and it could be a limited perspective because the real superpower of the human body is adaptability look at modern indigenous tribes the closest thing we have to natural humans and we see huge variations in their lifestyles and abilities the tarahumara tribe are capable of running distances of 200 miles in a single session the bajao sea nomads feature enlarged spleens that allow them to die for up to 13 minutes at a time the peraha people take naps of 15 minutes to 2 hours at most they don't sleep for a single stint which of these is natural and throughout our evolution we would have encountered countless more unique challenges and environments we are malleable and impermanent we now know that the brain is capable of rewiring itself in mass via brain plasticity to the extent that it's possible to lose an entire hemisphere and see enough rewiring in the remaining half of the brain to retain the majority of cognitive function to the extent that a blind person can learn to navigate their environment with sonar even our bones are constantly being broken down and reabsorbed they've been likened to banks for storing minerals all these abilities will allow us to evolve and to thrive in nearly any environment and this is why we can actually look at things like kyphosis anterior pelvic tilts obesity short attention spans and poor hip and ankle mobility as adaptive these are adaptations to sitting to surviving on plentiful albeit processed food to using the internet moreover unlike many cultures before us we've adapted our environments to us nearly everything in our environment is the perfect height such that we don't need to stoop or to climb we are lean mean sitting and walking machines that is not wrong but if you want to be able to kick ass if you want to be strong to be useful then this environment will develop a limited skill set many people will attempt to change this by returning to what they see as more natural movement patterns and lifestyles they do this with workouts that last 30 to 60 minutes four times a week training for three hours out of 168 each week is a drop in the ocean those movements are anomalies you're not giving your body the incentive to adapt because for the vast majority of the time it still doesn't need to so perhaps you push harder to try and create more stimulus in that short space of time and of course you injure yourself your body is not prepared for that kind of movement if you really want to trigger profound changes the need to change the environment change the environment change the organism because i mean your habits the way you move the way you think push yourself to keep learning and growing and don't be limited by what you think is natural for the human body your scope and potential is nearly limitless so the only question is what do you want to become so if you found this video useful and interesting guys something a little bit different if you did please leave a like and share around that helps me out immensely and if you like the idea of this uncommon training and a more philosophical approach to fitness then you might enjoy my ebook and training program super functional training you'll find a link to that in the description down below and there's currently a discount on whilst many of us are still stuck in lockdown be sure to check out grant's channel i'll put the link to that in the description down below as well he's now uploading weekly tutorials on various different martial arts moves and the first one on the spin hook kick is awesome so thanks a ton for watching guys hope you're all doing well and i'll see you soon bye for now

=== FILE: Training Philosophy： Why Train to be Stronger, Faster, Smarter [vZb7szZq_nY].en.txt ===

to many people fitness and performance simply means being really strong or maybe being able to run long distances but this isn't fitness this is simply being highly capable at a single task this doesn't prepare you for all the challenges life will throw at you and it doesn't develop your body and mind in a truly comprehensive and well-rounded manner it won't undo the significant damage caused by decades of sitting in the chair mildly stressed it's time to rethink what training can mean if you're professional athletes then I fully understand that sprinting lifting weights swimming diving or another sport is your career and your passion you have a genuine shot at being the very best in the world and therefore all your efforts should be focused on that one thing but for everyone else if the goal of training is to improve quality of life and physical and mental performance specialization doesn't make any sense at least not to me you tend to see this most often with weightlifting But this is an extremely limited explanation and it falls drastically short of explaining the true complexity of the process. Then there's short-term plasticity. Then there's the white glial cells that perform other important functions of the brain. There's the myriad neurotransmitters released from sacs at the end of each neuron during synaptic transmissions. These alter the excitability of neurons and their behaviour. There are likely many neurotransmitters that we have yet even to discover. There are the different resting states of different neurons, varied receptors for different brain regions. There's dendritic computation which shows us how a single neuron can handle basic computation on its own. There's the role of DNA and gene expression in processes like brain plasticity. And that means accepting compromise. And that means understanding what maximum performance looks like for you personally. There is no objective maximum performance. But then I stumbled on a concept from engineering that perfectly described the difficulty I was facing and provided a road map for how to move forward. The par frontier. So the parto frontier basically describes a set of multiple objectives and the hard limit of what can be achieved across those different goals. I recently watched a video on the subject from a channel called Universal Resilience where the presenter used a brilliant analogy that I'm going to borrow wholesale designing a Swiss Army knife. So, you see, a Swiss Army knife is an extremely useful tool because it's adaptable and can be handy in a variety of different situations. It's a knife, it's a screwdriver, it's a toothpick, and most importantly, it's small enough to fit into your pocket. But the catch is that the Swiss Army knife is not optimal for any one of its goals. The knife is small and relatively blunt. The screwdriver is fiddly and has a terrible grip. They'll work in a pinch, but they're not perfect in any scenario. Much better for cutting things then is an actual kitchen knife. The problem is that you can't make the knife on the Swiss Army knife much bigger, or it will take up space for one of the other tools, or it will make the Swiss Army knife less pocketable overall. You can't make progress towards one goal then without making sacrifices in another area. Just like a car designer might need to weigh up considerations like fuel efficiency, boot space, acceleration, top speed, price, repairability, all of which are competing to some extent. Now, a Swiss Army knife that has a bigger knife, better screwdriver, and more tools than another one, all while being the same size is objectively better, but there will come a point where the Swiss Army knife has achieved the perfect balance of traits, where the knife is as long as it can get without impacting on the other tools. Now it becomes a choice. Do you personally want a bigger knife or a better screwdriver? This is the Pareto frontier. The point where any meaningful progress towards one goal will necessarily result in compromise in another area. And at this point, Swiss Army knife A isn't better than Swiss Army knife B. Rather, it comes down to purely personal preference. Do you cut more or do you screw more? Now, let's apply this principle to training across multiple disciplines. Because if we're trying to max out our performance, we need to consider a large number of goals: strength, speed, endurance, mobility, reflexes, and skills. To an extent, we can train all of these things simultaneously and improve in every area. But there will come a time where we reach the Pareto frontier where we have maxed out each area as much as is possible without detracting from the others. And this is why I have never really been interested in traditional strength training. The myth that gets spread so often on social media is that getting strong is all you need. And the reason people say this is that they believe getting strong will make you better in all those other areas. Having a great strength potential will mean you can generate more power. It will mean you have more speed and explosiveness. Having greater strength will mean that you have more capacity for massive lifts, but also higher reps on smaller lifts. In other words, it'll boost your endurance in a sense. This is true to an extent and for a while, but eventually that changes. And at that point, getting stronger will actually eat into your endurance and your mobility. Once you become extremely strong, you'll probably be very heavy. That means it will take more energy to move, resulting in you getting more tired more quickly. After a certain point, this will also hurt your speed and your mobility and your agility. You also won't be optimizing for adaptations that could make you a better endurance athlete. Things like mitochondrial density, angioenesis, lung capacity, etc. You might be able to bench a lot of reps on a light weight, but this won't help you when you need to run more than 50 m. And this is borne out in Dragon Ball 2. When Golden Frieza takes on Goku, he probably has a massive power level, but he gets tired too quickly to be effective. Or how about when Future Trunks achieves Super Saiyan third grade against Cell? His power level is huge and he's impossibly strong, but that power level doesn't capture how this has affected his speed and he simply can't hit the much faster cell. Conversely, after a certain point, doing lots of long-distance running will start to break down muscle. So, you have to choose how much strength do you want and how much cardio. This is also why steroids are such a bad idea. Once athletes reach their limit, they will often take steroids to try and push further. Does this break through the Pareto frontier? No. It just hurts other areas that you maybe don't see. Things that are arguably more important like emotional stability, liver health, heart health, tendon strength, longevity, even facial attractiveness. Your body is eating itself to achieve more strength. There is always a cost. It's a mathematical certainty and it's why our body has these limits in the first place. It's not an accident. It's a design that evolved over billions of years because it's optimal. It's the optimal balance. Think a steroid abusing YouTuber is a better engineer than nature. And the problem isn't only that these things compete after a certain point. It's also that you only have so many hours in a day. You only have so much recovery capacity. So the time you're giving to your weightlifting is time you're not spending running. And you also have other non-training goals you need to consider. Just like the Swiss knife engineer needs to consider pocketability, weight, price, safety, marketability, we also need to consider outside factors like resources, time, being a good parent, work, interest levels. When deciding how much I can train towards my multiple goals, I need to consider how I'm going to balance that with spending time with my family, working on this channel, and enjoying my hobbies. Welcome to the Pareto Frontier. The good news is that you can treat this hard problem just like an engineer would by considering what's most important to you, what the goals you're trying to accomplish are, and how you want to look and feel. That is functional training. It's an entirely personal choice, but I will give you just one or two little pointers that might help you make key decisions. >> First, maxing out just one trait is always a mistake. While we've talked about strength and speed and mobility as these separate things, the truth is that they're actually just points on a gradient. They aren't separate categories at all. In fact, if you want to get a little bit philosophical, I don't really believe in categories in general, but perhaps that's a philosophical debate for another time. Any movement will require a combination of strength, endurance, mobility, intelligence, and coordination. If you completely neglect any one of these areas, you'll ultimately cease to be functional at all. Second, skills are your secret weapon. While you can't get infinitely stronger and infinitely faster, your ability to learn new skills and abilities is far less finite. In fact, it's limited really only by your time. I recently learned a simple queue that has massively improved my kicking ability, making them sharper and more powerful instantly at no cost to any of my other abilities. And those gains came much quicker than if I just tried to build leg strength. Manage your traits in accordance with the Pareto Frontier, but then stack those skills on top. And the great thing is that this is actually the message of Dragon Ball Z as it relates to power levels. Simply reading a number doesn't tell you anything about a fighter's abilities. Someone might have a much higher power level, but they can still be taken out by an amazing technique or just a little bit of tenacity. So, hope you enjoyed this video, guys. This video is sponsored by Squarespace, the website building platform that makes it extremely easy to get a website up and running. Guys, I just read this great article in Men's Health magazine all about science-based training and whether you can really outthink hard work. It was by some really smart guy, just so well written. I think his name was Adam Shannitzky. Seriously though, you should check it out. It was really fun to do some proper journalism again. For those of you who don't know, I was actually a full-time writer for many years, and there are a bunch of other great articles in the issue. I thought I'd use this as a jumping off point to relay some of those points and to discuss the trials and tribulations of science-based training a little bit further because it's a very hot topic on YouTube fitness right now. Some people saying that science-based training obviously is the way to go because science. And other people saying that it's overhyped, misguided, and often just a form of marketing. So, in this video, I'm going to deconstruct the argument, and I'm going to point out a contradiction that's at the very heart of science-based training. It's a tension that essentially makes it impossible for us to base our training precisely on studies and research, which isn't to say that science-based training is useless and that science has no place in training. We'll get to it, okay? We'll get there. So, what I always used to say was that science just means proof. Science is about testing theories, hypothesis in order to find out if they're accurate. So science-based training would make sense in this context. You can't say, "I don't believe in science." Because what you're really saying is, "I don't believe in proof." And I mean, to each their own. But when that science deniialism motivates someone to reject, say, life-saving medicine in favor of alternative remedies, it can actually be very dangerous. Worse if you start convincing other people of that viewpoint. And the same goes for supplements aimed at gymgoers or exciting new training methods. We need the science to tell us not to waste our money on things like BCAAs or turquestone. For the most part, we can't say anything completely conclusive, but we can look at studies and we can say, "Hey, maybe let's wait for more research before we spend our money." That's a good thing. That's where science-based training makes a lot of sense. I mean, maybe we shouldn't need studies to tell us not to take random things off the shelves because someone told us it was good, but apparently we kind of do. Likewise, science tells us that there's no such thing as spot reduction. It tells us that you can't just train your stomach to lose stomach fat. It doesn't work that way. And conversely, science-based training tells us when something does actually work. For example, we know that occlusion training, that's restricting blood flow to a particular muscle as you train it, can actually be beneficial for seeing greater gains using lighter weight. And this has a lot of use, for example, if you're someone who can't lift a lot of weight, if you're older, for example. And this is what science-based training sets out to do. It lets us separate the weak from the chaff, call out the charlatans, and find the methods that work versus the ones that don't. And it lets us discover new cuttingedge strategies to potentially gain even greater performance. So, what's not to like? Well, to play devil's advocate, you could say it was science-based training that introduced us to BCAAs and turquestone in the first place. You know, someone reads a study about a supplement, maybe they take it out of context, maybe it's an animal study, maybe it's not a great sample size, and then they just run with it and say this one study is now enough to prove that you should buy my product. That's not to say that the studies on those supplements were bad. It's to say that somebody saw an opportunity to market something because a study was out there. They took that information and ran with it. Cue the sweeping claims and the countless expensive supplements. And this is the problem with science-based training. It's not the studies themselves. It's not the idea of using science to guide our training. It's the way that those studies are applied and overapplied. So you can't have a problem with science as such. If you're building muscle and getting stronger, then you must be doing some science. You know, we don't build muscle through magic. So it must be science. The problem is using science as a marketing tool. But I would go further than that to say that almost anytime you refer to a study and say this means you should train this way, you are misapplying that science. Because in theory, science-based training training can show us the optimal angle to perform incline dumbbell presses for upper pec activation. It can show us the ideal number of sets and reps for hypertrophy. It can show us the ideal amount of time to rest between sets and the optimal amount of volume we need before we see diminishing returns. Except can it though? Because like I say, actually most studies can't be used to guide your training in any definitive kind of way. And it's not for any of the reasons that most videos critiquing science-based training focus on. It's not because of poor experimental design. It's not because of insufficient sample sizes. It's not because so many studies are based on animals. And it's not because of inherent bias in the studies. I mean, all those things are problems. Even when a study is designed perfectly, it still can't be applied in this way. So why not? Because of something called moderating variables. To understand these, we need to quickly brush up on the types of variables to see how moderating variables differ from confounding variables or independent variables. If that sounds very dry, I'm going to try and make it as straightforward as possible. So, variables are the conditions and factors that can be adjusted and measured in our experiments. So, let's imagine for example that a study shows that low reps build more muscle than high reps. The study takes two groups and measures their quads both before and after the study. During the study, the participants are prescribed leg extensions for either three sets of five or three sets of 30. That's the intervention. In this study, the rep range is the independent variable, the variable that we are adjusting in order to measure its effect. Quad growth is the dependent variable, the variable being affected that is showing us an effect. Participants from both groups are matched as easily as possible so that they have a similar age, similar average experience, etc. The researchers also need to control for other factors, making sure that the participants use a similar range of motion in their reps, use similar rest times, use a similar tempo. If the participants in one group, for example, were using a full range of motion and the others were all using a short range of motion, partial reps, just through sheer coincidence, that would be a confounding variable. So, you could no longer say with certainty that the observed outcome was the result of the rep ranges alone. It's unlikely this would happen, but it's possible, and so you can't rule it out unless you control for those variables. So to prevent this from happening, researchers need to teach participants to use full range of motion in both groups during the study, removing the confounder. So range of motion would have been a confounding variable. You know, one that you don't want that's going to mess up your results. But now it's a controlled variable instead, one that we're aware of and we're controlling. A lot of studies do make mistakes like this. Arguably, most will miss some of the most important confounding variables and will therefore have some limited usefulness. And this is one of the critiques we see most often. I mean, how many of these studies strictly control range of motion and tempo and every other aspect of training? They don't. And that's one of the reasons people critique them. But like I said, that's kind of missing the point. And that's where all this discourse around science-based training is just going round and round in circles. Because let's say that the study did control for all those variables. It was really welldesigned. Then a science-based fitness creator might see the study and make a video with the title, "Science finally proves that low rep Training is superior." You can't argue with science after all. And anyone looking at the study and how watertight it is would be forced to come to the same conclusion. But that would be a mistake because the very act of removing the confounding variables means that you're also removing potential moderators, which is a variable that can alter the result. More precisely, a variable that could alter the direction or the strength of the effect shown. Put it this way, what if hypothetically low rep training works best with a large range of motion. High rep training works best with a short range of motion. The study as designed would never tell us this even though it has by all accounts been designed well. And so somebody might be training high rep with a shorter range of motion and getting great results wondering why a science influencer is telling them that their method doesn't work. It's like yes under these conditions you get this result but if you do them slightly differently or slightly differently or slightly differently you get different results. So you haven't really proven anything about rep ranges. You've only proved something about rep ranges under very specific conditions, and not everyone's going to train that way. You haven't trained the myriad other options and combinations. And it gets way more muddy because there are way more potential moderating variables that would once again change up the results. What if, for example, the researchers had chosen to target a different muscle group, say the biceps. Different muscle groups have different leverage profiles. They contain variable ratios of fast twitch fibers to slow twitch fibers. So, it's very conceivable that this might affect the results. Here, muscle group selection is another pertinent moderating variable. How about tempo? Maybe high rep training works best with a faster tempo. If you don't control for that in the original study, then tempo could be a confounding variable. But if you do control for it, now you don't know whether changing your tempo would have altered the results, which would be useful information. Now, you've only proven that low rep training works best with your quadriceps using a full range of motion and a slow tempo, which means that you might be missing out on an even better way to grow your legs by using a higher rep range with a fast tempo and a short range of motion. And maybe that only works on certain muscle groups. Again, this is with a well-designed study. They could say this is where you get like a review of lots of studies, but you'd need countless millions of studies to cover every possible scenario. What if doing both highrep training and low rep training used simultaneously would result in the very best results of all? If this is true, and it probably is if you ask me, then none of the studies comparing the two will ever discover the most powerful option for building muscle at all. And just studies like this don't tend to exist. They're always comparing this to that. I think it's a kind of human tendency to like to categorize everything neatly, to try and compare everything, rank everything, which isn't how biology works. Biology is spectrums. It's multiffactorial. We can't just take two things and compare them and say job done. It's better to understand the mechanisms of how they work and to infer results and then test them that way. And that's before we've considered all of the really obvious stuff like individual differences, age, sex, experience, genetic predispositions. Again, this is stuff we should be controlling for. But by controlling for it, we don't see how different groups might benefit from different types of training. And what if it matters the order that you do things in? What if training with high repetitions originally will increase vascularization and work capacity so that you then get better results from low rep training? What if switching the order around gets the best results? Again, none of this is going to be borne out in these kinds of studies. By making studies watertight, we also make them far less nuanced and thereby not particularly useful, at least not for guiding and designing workouts. But to be clear, the researchers are not at fault here. The fault lies with the influencers and the articles that proclaim method X is better than method Y. This is never the intended purpose of the research. Not if it's done well by good researchers. Most credible scientists will just roll their eyes at such sweeping claims. Their conclusions don't end with you should train this way. They end with here's something else we need to study. Training variables are not better or worse. Rather, their effectiveness is moderated by countless interacting factors. The most interesting of which are actively removed, ironically, in good experimental design. It's a kind of moderator confounder tension, if you want to give it a name. So, if all that's true, then what are we to do? Do we just throw out science-based training and just trust the bros? You're not better off asking the guy down the gym who doesn't know what he's doing. As I discussed at the start of this article, there are scenarios where studies and research can be really useful to help us navigate these murky waters to test claims and to get an idea of things that we can try. Moreover, reading the studies can be really interesting. I talk a fair amount of science on this channel because I love learning about human performance and how the body works. And crucially understanding a bit about the nervous system and about chemistry and about biomechanics that helps me to better implement my ideas and to better assess the studies by understanding what's actually going on and what might have been missed. My degree was in psychology. We did a lot of neuroscience and learning about the nervous system has actually massively helped me to understand and interpret these studies. But when it comes to your actual training, there is another deep truth that most people just completely neglect as they get lost in the weeds, as they get lost in the argument of science versus bro science. And that is we don't need to optimize. These studies are aimed at top level athletes and coaches who want to squeeze out 1% extra performance in a very narrow field. Most likely, they're aimed at rehabilitating people with very specific injuries and conditions, and they're intended to add to a general body of knowledge to be referenced for future research. They're not meant to be dictating what we do at the gym. And as I've said in a previous video, you can get very good results with high reps, low reps, rapid cadence, slow cadence, heavyweight, lightweight. You know this is true because of the countless people arguing for each method as though their lives depended on it because they got good results because some of the people they coached got good results. Your job is to find the training style that works best for you individually. That means what you respond to based on your genetics, but it also means what you're able to implement, what you actually enjoy, which is ultimately far more important. You know, it doesn't matter if something's 1% more effective if you hate it and you're never going to do it. For me, the key has always been finding a way to feel the stimulus. With practice, you learn to feel what's working through experience. Sometimes that means getting more of a stretch in a movement. Sometimes it means getting more of a pump with high reps. And with experience, you can make nearly anything work. When someone tells you that your rest periods are wrong, and slightly longer rest periods would be optimal. For everyone else, just doing something's going to build muscle. And maybe you could be doing it 1% faster, but who cares? This is a big distinction I've been trying to make on the channel lately. The difference between fitness and niche bodybuilding. If you want to get fitter, and that includes getting a really decent physique, you don't need to worry about any of this. It can show us the ideal amount of time to rest between sets and the optimal amount of volume we need before we see diminishing returns. Except, can it though? Because like I say, actually, most studies can't be used to guide your training in any definitive kind of way. And it's not for any of the reasons that most videos critiquing science-based training focus on. It's not because of poor experimental design. It's not because of insufficient sample sizes. It's not because so many studies are based on animals. And it's not because of inherent bias in the studies. I mean, all those things are problems. Even when a study is designed perfectly, it still can't be applied in this way. So why not? Because of something called moderating variables. To understand these, we need to quickly brush up on the types of variables to see how moderating variables differ from confounding variables or independent variables. If that sounds very dry, I'm going to try and make it as straightforward as possible. So variables are the conditions and factors that can be adjusted and measured in our experiments. So let's imagine, for example, that a study shows that low reps build more muscle than high reps. The study takes two groups and measures their quads both before and after the study. During the study, the participants are prescribed leg extensions for either three sets of five or three sets of 30. That's the intervention. In this study, the rep range is the independent variable, the variable that we are adjusting in order to measure its effect. Quad growth is the dependent variable, the variable being affected that is showing us an effect. Participants from both groups are matched as easily as possible so that they have a similar age, similar average experience, etc. The researchers also need to control for other factors, making sure that the participants use a similar range of motion in their reps, use similar rest times, use a similar tempo. If the participants in one group, for example, were using a full range of motion and the others were all using a short range of motion, partial reps, just through sheer coincidence, that would be a confounding variable. So you could no longer say with certainty that the observed outcome was the result of the rep ranges alone. It's unlikely this would happen, but it's possible, and so you can't rule it out unless you control for those variables. So to prevent this from happening, researchers need to teach participants use full range of motion in both groups during the study, removing the confounder. So range of motion would have been a confounding variable, you know, one that you don't want that's going to mess up your results, but now it's a controlled variable instead, one that we're aware of and we're controlling. A lot of studies do make mistakes like this. Arguably most will miss some of the most important confounding variables and will therefore have some unlimited usefulness, and this is one of the critiques we see most often. I mean, how many of these studies strictly control range of motion and tempo and every other aspect of training? They don't. And that's one of the reasons people critique them. But like I said, that's kind of missing the point, and that's where all this discourse around science-based training is just going round and round in circles. Because let's say that the study did control for those variables, it was really well designed, then a science-based fitness creator might see the study and make a video with the title, Science Finally Proves That Low Rep Training Is Superior. You can't argue with science after all, and anyone looking at the study and how watertight it is would be forced to come to the same conclusion. But that would be a mistake, because the very act of removing the confounding variables means that you're also removing potential moderators, which is a variable that can alter the result. More precisely, a variable that could alter the direction or the strength of the effect shown. Put it this way, what if, hypothetically, low rep training works best with a large range of motion? High rep training works best with a short range of motion. The study, as designed, would never tell us this, even though it has by all accounts been designed well. And so somebody might be training high rep with a shorter range of motion and getting great results, wondering why a science influencer is telling them that their method doesn't work. It's like, yes, under these conditions you get this result, but if you do them slightly differently or slightly differently or slightly differently, you get different results. So you haven't really proven anything about rep ranges. You've only proved something about rep ranges under very specific conditions, and not everyone's going to train that way. You haven't trained the myriad other options and combinations. And it gets way more muddy, because there are way more potential moderating variables that would once again change up the results. What if, for example, the researchers had chosen to target a different muscle group, say the biceps? Different muscle groups have different leverage profiles. They contain variable ratios of fast twitch fibers to slow twitch fibers. So it's very conceivable that this might affect the results. Here, muscle group selection is another pertinent moderating variable. How about tempo? Maybe high rep training works best with a faster tempo. If you don't control for that in the original study, then tempo could be a confounding variable. But if you do control for it, now you don't know whether changing your tempo would have altered the results, which would be useful information. Now you've only proven that low rep training works best with your quadriceps, using a full range of motion and a slow tempo, which means that you might be missing out on an even better way to grow your legs by using a higher rep range with a fast tempo and a short range of motion. And maybe that only works on certain muscle groups. Again, this is with a well-designed study. They could say this is where you get like a review of lots of studies, but you'd need countless millions of studies to cover every possible scenario. What if doing both high rep training and low rep training used simultaneously would result in the very best results of all? If this is true, and it probably is if you ask me, then none of the studies comparing the two will ever discover the most powerful option for building muscle at all. And just studies like this don't tend to exist. They're always comparing this to that. I think it's a kind of human tendency to like to categorize everything neatly, to try and compare everything, rank everything, which isn't how biology works. Biology is spectrums. It's multifactorial. We can't just take two things and compare them and say, job done. It's better to understand the mechanisms of how they work and to infer results and then test them that way. And that's before we've considered all of the really obvious stuff like individual differences, age, sex, experience, genetic predispositions. Again, this is stuff we should be controlling for, but by controlling for it, we don't see how different groups might benefit from different types of training. And what if it matters the order that you do things in? What if training with high repetitions originally will increase vascularization and work capacity so that you then get better results from low rep training? What if switching the order around gets the best results? Again, none of this is going to be borne out in these kinds of studies. By making studies watertight, we also make them far less nuanced and thereby not particularly useful, at least not for guiding and designing workouts. But to be clear, the researchers are not at fault here. The fault lies with the influencers and the articles that proclaim method X is better than method Y. This is never the intended purpose of the research, not if it's done well by good researchers. Most credible scientists will just roll their eyes at such sweeping claims. Their conclusions don't end with, you should train this way. They end with, here's something else we need to study. Training variables are not better or worse. Rather, their effectiveness is moderated by countless interacting factors, the most interesting of which are actively removed, ironically, in good experimental design. It's a kind of moderator confounder tension, if you want to give it a name. So if all that's true, then what are we to do? Do we just throw out science-based training and just trust the bros? You're not better off asking the guy down the gym who doesn't know what he's doing.
